h1: Illinois HOA Special Assessment Challenge Letter Generator
metaTitle: Illinois HOA Special Assessment Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Challenge an unfair HOA special assessment in Illinois. Generate a state-specific demand letter citing the Common Interest Community Association Act today.
statuteCitation: 765 ILCS 160/1-45 (Common Interest Community Association Act); 765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8) (Illinois Condominium Property Act)
deadline: Owners with 20% of the votes may petition within 14 days (common interest communities, 765 ILCS 160/1-45(c)) or 21 days (condominiums, 765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8)) after the board action
penalty: A budget or separate assessment that would push total assessments above 115% of the prior fiscal year's can be put to an owner meeting, where it is rejected only if a majority of the total votes are cast to reject it
introParagraph: If your Illinois HOA or condominium association has hit you with a surprise special assessment, you have real legal rights to push back. Illinois law strictly regulates how boards must notice, vote on, and impose special assessments, and homeowners have specific tools to challenge assessments that exceed statutory limits or were adopted without proper procedure. A well-drafted demand letter citing the Common Interest Community Association Act or the Illinois Condominium Property Act often resolves disputes before they reach court. Boards know that improperly noticed or excessive assessments can be voided, and most associations would rather correct course than face litigation, attorney fees, and owner revolts. This page explains your rights and helps you generate a letter that gets results.
lawExplanation: Illinois protects homeowners from runaway special assessments through two primary statutes. For condominiums, Section 18(a)(8) of the Illinois Condominium Property Act (765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8)) requires that assessments for additions and alterations to the common elements or to association-owned property that are not included in the adopted annual budget be separately assessed and approved by two-thirds of the total votes of all unit owners. If an adopted budget or separate assessment would push the total regular and separate assessments for the current fiscal year above 115% of the preceding year's, owners holding 20% of the votes can deliver a petition within 21 days after the board action, and the board must then call a meeting within 30 days; unless a majority of the total votes are cast to reject it, the budget or assessment is ratified. For non-condo common interest communities (townhomes, master-planned HOAs), the Common Interest Community Association Act (765 ILCS 160/1-45) provides parallel protections. Condominium unit owners must receive notice of any board meeting concerning the adoption of the budget, regular assessments, or a separate (special) assessment (765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8)(i)), and in a common interest community the board must give members notice of such a meeting 10 to 60 days beforehand (765 ILCS 160/1-40(b)(4)). Assessments adopted without that notice may be open to challenge. Condominium board members must exercise the care required of a fiduciary of the unit owners (765 ILCS 605/18.4), and in a common interest community a contract with a board member or a business in which a member has a 25% or greater interest is restricted by 765 ILCS 160/1-30(b), so self-dealing or undisclosed conflicts can be challenged. Importantly, separate assessments for expenditures relating to emergencies or mandated by law may be adopted by the board without owner approval or the 115% petition procedure (765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8)(iv); 765 ILCS 160/1-45(e)), but they must fit the statutory definition of an emergency. Procedural defects—improper notice, lack of quorum, missing meeting minutes, or failure to provide the financial basis for the assessment—are common grounds for challenge.
letterStrategy: An effective Illinois HOA special assessment challenge letter does three things: identifies the specific statutory violation, demands a concrete remedy with a deadline, and signals that you understand your litigation options. Start by citing the exact statute that applies to your community—765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8) for condos or 765 ILCS 160/1-45 for other common interest communities. State the date of the board action, the amount of the assessment, and the procedural or substantive defect: insufficient notice, exceeding the 115% threshold without owner approval, lack of itemized justification, or absence of a properly noticed meeting. Reference the board's statutory duties and request inspection of records under 765 ILCS 605/19 or 765 ILCS 160/1-30(i), which give you the right to review association records on written request; a condominium board that does not make requested records available within 10 business days is deemed to have denied the request (a common interest community board has 30 days). Demand specific relief: rescission of the assessment, a properly noticed re-vote, refund of any amounts already paid, or production of records. Set a 14- to 30-day deadline for response. Most Illinois boards consult counsel when they receive a citation-laden letter, and many will negotiate rather than risk a declaratory judgment action or owner petition drive. Keep the tone firm and factual—not emotional. Send by certified mail with return receipt to create a paper trail, and copy the property manager and association attorney if known.
proceduralNotes: If your demand letter does not resolve the dispute, Illinois homeowners can sue in circuit court for declaratory and injunctive relief, and small claims court handles disputes up to $10,000. Actions on written contracts are subject to a ten-year limitation (735 ILCS 5/13-206), but challenges to specific board actions should be brought promptly to avoid laches. Always preserve evidence of notice deficiencies and request records in writing before filing.

faq.q: Can my Illinois HOA impose a special assessment without owner approval?
faq.a: Sometimes. Boards can adopt special assessments, but if the total assessments for the year would exceed 115% of the prior year's, owners holding 20% of the votes can petition (within 14 days in a common interest community, within 21 days in a condominium) to force an owner meeting, and a majority of the total votes can reject the assessment. Assessments for additions or alterations not in the budget need owner approval (two-thirds of the total votes in a condominium; a simple majority of members in a common interest community). Emergency assessments, and assessments mandated by law, are exempt from the petition procedure but must fit the statutory definition of an emergency.

faq.q: How much notice must my Illinois HOA give before voting on a special assessment?
faq.a: Condominium unit owners must receive notice of any board meeting concerning the adoption of a separate assessment (765 ILCS 605/18(a)(8)(i)), and condominium board meetings must also be posted at least 48 hours ahead (765 ILCS 605/18(a)(9)). In a common interest community the board must give members notice of a meeting on a special assessment 10 to 60 days beforehand (765 ILCS 160/1-40(b)(4)). Board meetings must generally be open to unit owners; the statutory closed-session topics do not include adopting an assessment. If your board adopted the assessment without proper notice or behind closed doors, that procedural defect is strong grounds to challenge the assessment in your demand letter.

faq.q: What records can I demand from my HOA before challenging a special assessment?
faq.a: Illinois law gives you broad inspection rights. Under 765 ILCS 605/19 (condos) and 765 ILCS 160/1-30(i) (CICAA), you can request governing documents, minutes, financial records, contracts, and reserve studies. A condominium board that does not make requested records available within 10 business days is deemed to have denied the request, and a common interest community board has 30 days. Make your request in writing, state with particularity the records you want, and state a proper purpose where the statute requires one. If they refuse or stall, a member who prevails in an action to compel production is entitled to attorney's fees and costs, which adds leverage to your demand letter.

faq.q: Can I withhold payment of a contested special assessment in Illinois?
faq.a: Generally no—withholding payment is risky. Illinois associations can record liens for unpaid assessments and may foreclose, plus they can recover attorney fees and costs. The safer approach is to pay under written protest while pursuing your challenge, or to negotiate an escrow arrangement. Some homeowners pursue a declaratory judgment action to halt collection while the dispute is resolved. Always consult counsel before withholding, and use a strong demand letter first to attempt resolution without escalation.

faq.q: What if my HOA retaliates after I challenge the assessment?
faq.a: Retaliation by an Illinois HOA—selective fines, denial of amenities, harassment—may support claims for breach of the declaration, a challenge to any fine imposed without notice and an opportunity to be heard (765 ILCS 605/18.4(l); 765 ILCS 160/1-30(g)), or even fair-housing claims if discriminatory. Document every interaction, save written communications, and request records showing how similar issues were handled for other owners. Retaliation evidence often strengthens your underlying assessment challenge and may justify additional relief in court.
